claims.text: Modular sub-components for decision-making, planning, and control perform poorly in out-of-distribution test-time scenarios.
Foundation models deployed to decision-making tasks are prone to hallucination.
Hallucinations in decision-making foundation models produce decisions that sound reasonable but are poor in practice.
A general definition for hallucinations in foundation models applied to decision-making tasks is provided alongside examples and mitigation guidelines.

evidence.description: Hand-engineered or learning-based decision-making sub-components perform well in designed situations but perform poorly in out-of-distribution test-time scenarios.
While foundation models show promising results in decision-making, they are known to hallucinate during execution.
Foundation models generate decisions that may sound reasonable but are in fact poor.
The work provides a general definition for hallucinations, reviews existing hallucination detection and mitigation techniques for decision problems, and presents guidelines.

methodologies.name: Literature Survey and Conceptual Framework Definition
methodologies.description: Systematic review and taxonomy definition of hallucination use cases, detection, and mitigation methods for foundation models in decision-making tasks.

limitations.text: Hand-engineered and learning-based decision-making algorithms perform poorly in out-of-distribution scenarios at test-time.
Foundation models used for decision-making hallucinate and generate decisions that sound plausible but are incorrect or unsafe.

future_work.text: Design systems that can simultaneously quantify the certainty of a model's decision and detect when it may be hallucinating in decision-making tasks.
